abstract: Background: Tuberculosis imposes a major public-health burden in Africa, while variation in isoniazid and rifampicin disposition creates opportunities for improved pharmacotherapy. The population architecture of extended, phased pharmacogenomic backgrounds remains less well characterized than individual marker frequencies. Methods: We analyzed high-coverage, phased GRCh38 genomes from 661 unrelated individuals sampled from five continental-African and two African-diaspora populations at NAT2, SLCO1B1, CES2, HLA-B, NR1I2 and UGT1A1. We integrated frequency differentiation, reduced phased signatures, linkage disequilibrium, functional annotation and NAT2 core-allele inference with individual-clustered permutation tests. Results: The six loci contributed 17,223 annotated variant records and 276 entries in a capped frequency-differentiation register. Exact NAT2 core-definition matching was achieved for 1,321/1,322 chromosomes (99.92%), and determinate genotype-inferred acetylator categories for 620/661 individuals (93.80%). Among the sampled continental-African populations, 35-site noncore background distributions differed within NAT2 *5 (BH-adjusted q=0.000100), *4 (q=0.024733) and *6 (q=0.000350) groups. Distinct phased and linkage architectures also characterized transporter, hydrolysis, regulatory and HLA-B genomic regions. Conclusion: African population-associated variation extends beyond commonly used pharmacogenetic allele definitions. The observed NAT2 backgrounds and complementary locus signatures provide a foundation for targeted molecular studies and prospective pharmacokinetic validation that could inform future population-responsive TB treatment research.
